name_en: Fu Shou Shan High Mountain Oolong
processing: Very lightly oxidised (around 10–15%), ball-rolled and gently dried with no roast; the farm's own lots are processed in small batches from a few hectares of garden.
harvest_season: A late-spring pick in June and a smaller winter crop in October; the altitude allows no more than two harvests a year.
appearance_dry: Dense, tightly rolled balls in a deep jade green, heavy and glossy, with a sweet, orchard-like dry aroma.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold with a green tint, thick and bright.
appearance_wet: Thick, whole, rubbery leaves in a uniform deep green with barely a trace of red at the edge.
taste_profile: Pear and apple sweetness that seems borrowed from the orchards next door, white flowers, a thick, almost syrupy texture and a cooling finish that lasts.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, a generous dose and a long first steep to open the balls. If the leaf is clean, skip the rinse and taste the very first infusion; it is often the most aromatic.

vintage_note: The farm sells its own tea by harvest, the June and October picks of the current year, in sealed, labelled packs in limited quantity, mostly at the farm and a few outlets. Everything else sold as Fushoushan is at best from neighbouring Lishan gardens of similar altitude (Hua Gang and Cui Luan are the usual sources). Both are fresh teas meant for drinking within the year, never aged.
description:
Fu Shou Shan is a farm, not a mountain: Fushoushan Farm, run by Taiwan's Veterans Affairs Council on the heights above Lishan at roughly 2,100 to 2,600 metres, originally set up to give retired servicemen work growing temperate fruit. Its small tea gardens, among the highest still in production in Taiwan, make a Qing Xin oolong that has become one of the most prized names in the country.

The tea is made the high-mountain way, very lightly oxidised, ball-rolled and unroasted, and the altitude does the rest. The leaves grow slowly through cold nights, and the cup is dense and sweet in the way only the top gardens manage: pear and apple notes that seem to borrow from the orchards next door, white flowers, a thick, almost syrupy texture and a cooling finish that lasts.

Brew it generously with water straight off the boil, give the tight balls a long first steep, and expect ten infusions from good leaf. It is subtle rather than loud, so skip the rinse if the leaf is clean and taste the very first infusion; it is often the most aromatic.

The farm sells its own tea in sealed, labelled packaging, in limited quantities and mostly at the farm itself and a few outlets, which is the only way to be sure you have farm-grown Fu Shou Shan. Everything else labelled Fushoushan is, at best, from neighbouring Lishan gardens at similar altitude (Hua Gang and Cui Luan are the usual sources) and at worst from much lower. Harvests are late spring (June) and a smaller winter crop in October; the tea is sold by harvest and meant to be drunk fresh, within the year.

If you cannot get the farm's own, a well-sourced Hua Gang or Cui Luan lot will give you most of the same experience at a kinder price.
history:
Fu Shou Shan takes its name from a state-linked farm above Lishan, better known at first for temperate fruit than for tea. Its small gardens came to stand for the top of Taiwan's high-mountain oolong, and the name now reaches well beyond the farm's own output.

Little is documented in detail about when tea planting began there or how large the gardens are, so altitude and acreage figures should be read as approximate.
